life_dates_and_posts: b. 11 September 1954, New Haven (CV p. 1; Wikidata P569). B.A. Wisconsin–Madison 1976; Rhodes Scholar 1976–78; D.Phil. Oxford 1981; Ph.D. Yale December 1990. Yale 1981–92 (tenured 1988); Frederick Jackson Turner Professor, Wisconsin–Madison, 1992–2003; Turner and Vilas Research Professor 2003–20; emeritus 2020–. ASEH president 1989–93; Weyerhaeuser Environmental Books series editor 1994–2014; AHA vice-president 2002–05 and president 2012–13 (CV pp. 1–2, 14–15).

people_update.label: William Cronon
people_update.identity_note: American environmental historian, b. 11 September 1954, New Haven; Yale 1981–92; University of Wisconsin–Madison 1992–2020 (Frederick Jackson Turner and Vilas Research Professor), emeritus; president of the ASEH 1989–93 and of the AHA 2012–13. Wikidata Q8007305 confirmed by QLever on 2026-10-23 (the sheet's bulk match of 2026-09-22 is thereby reviewed).

proposed_edges.relationship: The wilderness debate: Hays found 'a world of abstracted ideas … divorced from the values and ideas inherent in wilderness action' (1996, as quoted by Foreman); Sessions, habitat underweighted (1996); Foreman, that the 'Received Wilderness Idea' of 'Callicott, Cronon and other postmodern deconstructionist scholars' is 'a straw dog; it does not exist on the ground' (1998; 2000)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Foreman 2000 read in full (data/extension-2026/period4-wave1-2026-10-23/evidence-environment.md §2.2): pp. 32–33 and the reference list p. 38. Hays's sentence is carried only as quoted by Foreman (p. 32); Hays's comment (Environmental History 1:1, 29–32) is unread and the quotation is marked for re-verification. Sessions 1996 read in full (graph record). Callicott and Nelson 1998 known by publisher description and Foreman's own reference. Cronon's 1996 response (pp. 47–55) is unread: this edge records the critics' words; his 1995 defence of wild-land protection and nonhuman autonomy is on cronon_wilderness (reflow pp. 12, 17–20). Source strand environment/wilderness_debate.

proposed_edges.relationship: Wilderness as the erasure of Indigenous dwelling: 'The removal of Indians to create an "uninhabited wilderness"' shows 'just how invented, just how constructed, the American wilderness really is' (1995); the Apostle Islands, 'inhabited by Ojibwe peoples for centuries', 'a wilderness that has long been a place of human dwelling' (2003)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Own words. 1995: author-hosted reflow p. 10 (graph record cronon_wilderness, read in full 2026-10-13). 2003: 'The Riddle of the Apostle Islands', read in full in OCR (data/extension-2026/period4-wave1-2026-10-23/evidence-environment.md §2.2, P6): the Ojibwe sentence on the scan's third page (Orion p. 38), 'a wilderness that has long been a place of human dwelling' and 'manage the Apostle Islands as a historical wilderness' (p. 39). Warren (1997) and Jacoby (2001), his doctoral students (CV p. 11), and Spence (1999, abstract read) wrote on the same removal; nothing read here connects their books to this essay, so they are named as context only. Target strand indigenous/land ('Land, identity and colonial change').

proposed_edges.relationship: History for land managers and the public: the Apostle Islands should be managed 'as a historical wilderness' whose policy 'should equally protect stories—stories of wild nature, stories of human history' (2003); as AHA president he asked historians to 'connect our professional stories with the concerns of the wider public' (2013)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Own words. 2003 essay read in full in OCR (data/extension-2026/period4-wave1-2026-10-23/evidence-environment.md §2.2): the riddle passage (p. 39) and the closing paragraph ('It is a storied wilderness'). 2013 address: open AHA text, passages (data/extension-2026/period4-wave1-2026-10-23/evidence-environment.md §1.3). CV (read): Trust for Public Land board 2003–20; Wisconsin Historical Society curators 1997–2011; the 2012 column 'The Public Practice of History in and for a Digital Age' (title only). Target strand publichistory/place_preservation.

proposed_edges.relationship: 'The digital revolution has created endless opportunities via blogs, websites, YouTube, and social media' for the historian's stories (2013); presidential columns 'The Public Practice of History in and for a Digital Age' and 'Scholarly Authority in a Wikified World' (2012); 'digital scholarship' named among his fields
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Moderate. The 2013 sentence is read (open AHA text, data/extension-2026/period4-wave1-2026-10-23/evidence-environment.md §1.3); the 2012 Perspectives columns are known by title from the CV (p. 8) and his AHA-writings page; the CV (p. 1) lists 'digital scholarship' among his fields and (p. 10) the websites he built. The columns themselves are unread. No target strand: the entry's strands are per-work; the coordinator may attach it to the 2005 Cohen–Rosenzweig strand or leave it unattached.

proposed_edges.relationship: Leopold as teacher and model: the landscape-reading course he drew from Leopold (afterword, 2003), essays on Leopold and A Sand County Almanac (1998), and Leopold among the 'Classics and Precursors' of his reading list (2005)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Afterword pp. 173–175 (graph record cronon_changes_afterword, read: the Wisconsin landscape training and Leopold's course model); CV p. 9 (read): 'A Voice in the Wilderness: Aldo Leopold' (Wilderness, 1998) and 'A Sand County Almanac' in A Wisconsin Fifteen (1998), titles only; the 2005 reading list (graph record pe131_carson_cronon_readings_2005, read). Parallels edge_911 (leopold → environment), which already cites the afterword.

proposed_edges.relationship: 'Modes of Prophecy and Production' answered Worster's 1990 agroecological programme (unread; reported by Isenberg 2013); 'A Place for Stories' (1992) read Dust Bowl as a story whose 'chief agent' is capitalism and whose plot 'proclaims an apocalyptic prophecy', set against Bonnifield's progressive plot
proposed_edges.map_label: Prophecy and production: reading Dust Bowl, 1990–92
proposed_edges.evidence_note: 'A Place for Stories' pp. 1347–1349 and 1363–1364 read (graph record pe131_cronon_place_stories_1992): the 'chief agent' and 'apocalyptic prophecy' sentences are at p. 1363, Worster's few pages on Indians at p. 1364. The 1990 response (JAH 76:4, 1122–31) is unread (OUP 403) and is known through Isenberg 2013, pp. 88–89 (read, graph record pe131_crosby_isenberg_2013); Cronon's CV p. 7 confirms the citation. A critique by reading, not a rejection: Cronon's essay treats both plots as narrative choices.

edges_considered_not_proposed.reason: Co-authored 'Indians and the Land' (1986) and the Handbook chapter (1989), per the CV; White is wave 2.
No reader read here says so; the dissertation data are not edge evidence. The link between the entries is Agent B's p4B_rel_16.
No turner node; the 1987 WHQ essay and the Turner professorship stay in the chronology.
The Muir (1996) and Eiseley (2016) editions are editorial work, not biographical argument.

row.context: Held wilderness to be a cultural invention whose making required 'The removal of Indians to create an "uninhabited wilderness"' (1995) and asked that the Apostle Islands, 'inhabited by Ojibwe peoples for centuries', be managed 'as a historical wilderness' (2003). Spence (1999) examined Indian removal in the making of national parks.
row.works: 'The Trouble with Wilderness' (1995); 'The Riddle of the Apostle Islands' (2003)

row.context: Wrote for land managers and the public: the Apostle Islands as 'a storied wilderness' whose management 'should equally protect stories' (2003); as AHA president asked historians to 'connect our professional stories with the concerns of the wider public' (2013; passages read); Trust for Public Land board 2003–20.

As AHA president wrote on 'The Public Practice of History in and for a Digital Age' and 'Scholarly Authority in a Wikified World' (2012; titles only) and told the association that 'The digital revolution has created endless opportunities' for historians' stories (2013; passages read).
